analysis.one_liner: Expands federal workplace safety law to public employees and sharply raises penalties for employers who endanger workers.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 28, 2026 with 17 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate labor committee, the bill has received no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would expand the federal workplace safety law to cover state and local government employees, who are currently left out. It strengthens protections for workers who report injuries or refuse dangerous work, gives injured workers and their families rights to follow safety cases, and raises fines for unsafe employers tenfold or more, including criminal prison terms for executives in death cases. It was introduced in late April 2026 and referred to the Senate committee that handles labor issues, where it has sat with no hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers gain stronger protections in several ways: the roughly 8 million-plus state and local government employees not currently covered by the federal OSHA law would come under its protections, with a phase-in of up to 36 months for governments in states without their own approved plans [S2]. Whistleblowers who report injuries or refuse dangerous work would get reinstatement, back pay, damages, and attorney fees, with rights that cannot be waived by arbitration or employment agreements [S2]. Employees would be paid for time spent helping safety inspections [S2], and workers or their families would gain the right to meet with investigators, receive citations when employers do, and speak at settlement proceedings [S2]. Workers also gain from tenfold-higher civil fines, criminal penalties of up to 10 years in prison for knowing violations that cause a death, annual inflation adjustments so penalties do not erode, and a rule that no new standard can reduce existing protections [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Extends federal OSHA coverage to state and local government employees, who are currently excluded from the law, phased in over up to 36 months in states without approved plans

Gives workers who report injuries or refuse dangerous work strong remedies: reinstatement, back pay, compensatory damages, attorney fees, and anti-retaliation rights that cannot be waived by arbitration or employment contracts
Raises maximum civil penalties roughly tenfold, to $700,000 for willful or repeated violations and $70,000 per day for uncorrected serious violations, and indexes them to inflation each year

Creates criminal penalties of up to 10 years in prison for knowing violations that cause a worker's death (20 years for repeat offenders), reaching officers and directors personally, and up to 5 years for causing serious bodily harm

Gives injured workers and grieving families the right to meet with investigators, receive citations and reports when employers do, be heard before settlements, and get a designated family liaison at each OSHA area office

Bars employer policies that discourage injury reporting, requires prompt reporting of deaths, hospitalizations, amputations, and eye losses, and pays employees for time spent aiding safety inspections
Directs OSHA to update outdated national consensus safety standards within two years and forbids any new rule from weakening existing protections

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers bear higher civil penalties (up to $700,000 for willful or repeated violations and $70,000 per day for uncorrected serious violations), new injury-reporting and recordkeeping duties, and personal criminal exposure for officers and directors who knowingly violate safety rules and cause a death or serious injury. State and local governments, whose workers would newly be covered, would bear the cost of complying with federal safety standards, and state-run safety programs could face federal reassertion of enforcement if they fall short. Some of these costs would flow to consumers and taxpayers through prices and public budgets.

drawbacks.text: The tenfold penalty increases and new criminal liability for officers and directors would raise compliance and insurance costs, which fall hardest on small employers and can be passed to consumers through prices
Extending OSHA to state and local governments would impose federal standards and inspection costs on public budgets, with a phase-in of up to 36 months in states without their own plans
Allowing the federal government to reassert enforcement over state-run safety programs shifts authority from states to Washington and could create overlapping inspections and conflicting requirements

Raising criminal penalties from six months to as much as 10 years for workplace deaths is a major expansion of criminal law that prosecutors and juries would have to apply to ordinary safety decisions
The bill directs extensive new enforcement activity, family liaisons, GAO reviews, and training grants without identified funding, which could strain OSHA's capacity

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to the roughly eight million public employees now outside federal safety law and to workers in high-fatality industries who would face employers with tenfold fines and, for the first time, real prison exposure for knowing violations that kill. The costs are real but comparatively modest: higher compliance spending by employers, some price effects for consumers, and added costs to state and local governments, plus a genuine federalism tradeoff in overriding weak state safety programs. The main weakness is not design but prospects: a bill of this scope ordinarily needs hearings, cost estimates, and bipartisan negotiation, none of which has begun.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee on the day it was introduced and has sat there since, with no hearing or vote scheduled while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 28, 2026 by Senator Sanders with 17 Democratic cosponsors
It was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
No hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since referral
The bill would expand OSHA coverage to state and local government employees, with up to a 36-month phase-in for governments in states without approved plans
It raises civil penalties roughly tenfold and adds criminal penalties of up to 10 years for knowing violations causing a worker's death, rising to 20 years for repeat convictions
It gives whistleblowers reinstatement, damages, and attorney fees, and gives injured workers and families rights to participate in investigations and settlements

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: At this stage, no one has gained yet: workers' protections are unchanged while the bill waits in committee, and employers continue to face today's lower penalties and the current scope of the law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; employers keep status quo

sides.party_line_note: The bill is sponsored by an independent senator who caucuses with Democrats plus 17 Democratic cosponsors, with no Republican support in the record.

industries.industry: Employers in hazardous industries (construction, manufacturing, warehousing, meatpacking)
industries.note: The bill multiplies the financial and criminal consequences of safety violations, raising the maximum willful/repeat fine from $70,000 to $700,000 and imposing up to 10-year prison terms on officers and directors for knowing violations that kill a worker. Employers' interest in lower enforcement costs runs against the bill's worker-safety aims.

The bill lets federal OSHA reassert concurrent enforcement authority whenever it finds a state plan is failing, and requires repeated-violation findings to count an employer's record across all states. State programs' interest in operating independently runs against the bill's stronger federal oversight.

industries.industry: State and local governments as employers
industries.note: Government workplaces would be subject to federal OSHA standards, inspections, and penalties for the first time, phased in over up to 36 months, adding compliance costs that state and local budgets would absorb.

The bill requires annual electronic reporting of injury data in a searchable public format and a site log covering contractors at multi-employer worksites, reducing employers' control over injury information. These rules serve worker and public awareness rather than employer interests.

analysis.trajectory: The bill faces long odds: it has no Republican cosponsors and sits in a committee whose agenda is controlled by the majority party. The Protecting America's Workers Act has been introduced repeatedly over roughly 15 years without reaching either chamber's floor. Barring a major workplace disaster that creates political pressure, the most likely path is that it stays in committee until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027. Even in a Democratic-controlled Senate, comparable OSHA penalty and coverage expansions have stalled; the current chamber composition makes floor action unlikely.
